title: Possessive Articles in Dative
objectives: I can find the subject, the accusative object and the dative object in a sentence
I can use mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser and euer in the dative
I can add -n to plural nouns in the dative
I can build sentences like Ich gebe meinem Mann einen Kuss

grammar.title: Subject, direct object, indirect object
grammar.body:
In *Ich gebe meinem Mann einen Kuss* there are three parts:

**ich** = subject (nominative). **einen Kuss** = direct object (accusative). **meinem Mann** = indirect object (dative).

The indirect object is the **recipient** of the direct object: the husband receives the kiss. The dative object is the one that changes to the dative form, and with a possessive article (mein, dein ...) the endings are the same as for *einem, einer*.
grammar.ar: المفعول به غير المباشر (من يستلم الشيء) يكون في حالة Dativ.

grammar.title: Endings of possessive articles in dative
grammar.body:
Take the possessive article that matches the owner (ich → mein, du → dein, er/es → sein, sie → ihr, wir → unser, ihr → euer, Sie → Ihr). Then add the ending that matches the gender of the **dative noun**:

**masculine: -em**, **neuter: -em**, **feminine: -er**, **plural: -en**.

In the plural, the **noun** also gets an extra **-n**: *die Kinder* → *meinen Kindern*, *die Freunde* → *seinen Freunden*. If the plural noun already ends in -n, nothing is added: *meinen Nachbarn*, *unseren Großeltern*.

*euer* drops the middle *e* when an ending is added: *eurem, eurer, euren*. Also *unser* is used as *unserem, unserer, unseren*.
grammar.ar: المذكر والمحايد: em ، المؤنث: er ، الجمع: en + إضافة n للاسم.

grammar.title: Examples with sein, ihr and unser
grammar.body: Martin is masculine, so we use **sein**; Maria is feminine, so we use **ihr**; Lukas and Katharina are 'we', so we use **unser**. Then the dative ending depends on the person who receives.

mistakes.wrong: Ich gebe meine Tochter einen Kuss.
mistakes.right: Ich gebe meiner Tochter einen Kuss.
mistakes.why: The person who receives is dative: feminine = *-er*.

mistakes.wrong: Ich gebe meinen Kinder einen Kuss.
mistakes.right: Ich gebe meinen Kindern einen Kuss.
mistakes.why: In the dative plural the noun gets an extra *-n*.

mistakes.wrong: Er kauft seinen Frau eine Schokolade.
mistakes.right: Er kauft seiner Frau eine Schokolade.
mistakes.why: *Frau* is singular and feminine, so *seiner*, not *seinen*.

pronunciation.tip: At the end of *meiner, deiner, seiner* the *-er* sounds like a short 'a': 'mai-na'.
In *Küsse* and *Bücher* round your lips as for 'oo' and say 'ee'.

lines.en: I am buying my father a book. And you?

lines.de: Ich bringe meinen Eltern einen Wein.
lines.en: I am bringing my parents a wine.

tip: Think of einem / einer / einen: the possessive endings in dative are exactly the same, just with mein-, dein- ... in front.

comprehension.q: Which endings do possessive articles take in the dative?

comprehension.a: The recipient of the direct object, for example meinem Mann in: Ich gebe meinem Mann einen Kuss.

comprehension.q: What happens to a plural noun in the dative?
comprehension.a: It gets an extra -n (Kindern), unless it already ends in -n.

comprehension.q: Why do we say 'unseren Großeltern' and not 'unseren Großelternn'?

exercises.instructions: Write the possessive article in the dative.

summary: The indirect object (the recipient) is in the dative.
In the dative plural the noun gets -n unless it already ends in -n.
The endings are the same as einem, einer.
